s: Hector sends Dolon (to explore the Greek fleet)
q: Extend The watch beyond the lines, and there receive Dolon our spy, who sallied forth t’ explore The navy of our foes

s: Chorus is a watching chorus (stationed during the night watch)
q: Wake! what means this long delay? Rise and watch; now dawns the day?

s: Dolon is a spy (for Hector and Troy)
q: Dolon our spy, who sallied forth t’ explore The navy of our foes

s: Dolon conducts Dolon’s reconnaissance (of the Greek fleet)
q: Dolon our spy, who sallied forth t’ explore The navy of our foes

s: Dolon’s reconnaissance targets the Greek fleet
q: Dolon our spy, who sallied forth t’ explore The navy of our foes

s: Troy is a beleaguered city (under Greek attack)
q: when from the foe We have delivered this beleaguered city

s: Achilles withstand thy vengeful hand
q: How shall Achilles’ self withstand, Or Ajax meet, thy vengeful hand?

s: Achilles refuses to assist the Greeks (because he is angry with the chiefs)
q: He sailed, And still is here, but angry with the chiefs, Refuses to assist them

s: Ajax be equal to Tydeus’ son
q: Ajax, I deem, and Tydeus’ son are equal To any

s: Ulysses is a Greek chief (fluent in speech and sufficiently courageous)
q: but most fluent in his speech, And with sufficient fortitude inspired, Is that Ulysses

s: Ulysses is stationed at Thymbræan temple (near the Trojan ramparts)
q: At the Thymbræan temple is he stationed Hard by our ramparts

s: Rhesus be exposed to such blasts (through Pæonia)
q: to such blasts As cover with thick ice the Thracian wave, Or through Pæonia howl, was I exposed

s: Ulysses is a spy (who entered Troy in disguise)
q: disguised In tattered vest, that vile impostor next Entered the gates, and cursed the Argive host, Sent as a spy to Ilion

s: Ulysses has stolen Minerva (by taking her image from her temple)
q: Entering Minerva’s fane, he stole her image, And bore it to the Grecian fleet

s: the Thracians serves Rhesus (as his army)
q: I had reached the Euxine shore To sail with Thracia’s host

s: night watch have assigned times The times assigned us
q: The times assigned us sentinels is o’er

s: Choræbus be chief of night watch
q: ’Tis said Choræbus, son of Mygdon, is their chief

s: Aurora be at hand Troy
q: Aurora is at hand

s: Rhesus subdue The people (to your empire)
q: When round Pangæum and Pæonia’s realm Rushing upon the hardiest Thracian troops I broke their ranks of battle, and subdued The people to your empire

s: Rhesus bind to pay them (annual tribute)
q: Having conquered them, and taken For hostages their children, them I bound To pay me annual tribute

s: Rhesus sail with Thracia’s host
q: I had reached the Euxine shore To sail with Thracia’s host

s: Rhesus has arrived at Troy (late, during the tenth year of the war)
q: But I, though late, am in due season come: For this is the tenth year since thou hast waged An ineffectual war

s: Rhesus is related to Hector (as a kinsman)
q: But you, our kinsman, who derive your birth From a barbarian stem

s: Rhesus was raised to throne (by Hector)
q: I raised you to the wide-extended throne

s: Ulysses is a Greek warrior
q: ULY. Heard’st thou, O Diomede, the sound of arms,

s: Minerva protects Ulysses (through many toils)
q: ULY. Dread goddess, O Minerva, I distinguished Thy well-known voice: for midst unnumbered toils Thou ever dost support me:

s: Minerva assumes the form of Venus (to delay Paris)
q: MIN. You can no more, the Destinies forbid: For Hector must not perish by your hand; But haste to him on whom ye came to wreak Fate’s dreadful purposes: myself meanwhile Assuming Venus’ form, who ’midst the toils Of battle by her tutelary care Protects him, will with empty words detain Paris your foe.

s: Rhesus is a king of Thrace
q: CHA. Ah! wretched me, and O thou king Of Thrace, who in an evil hour beheld’st Accursed Ilion; what an end of life Was thine!

s: Rhesus is son of the Muse (her dearest son)
q: MUSE. Ye Trojans, mark me well: for I a Muse Who by the wise am worshipped, hither come, One of the nine famed sisters, having seen The wretched fate of this my dearest son, Who by the foe was slain:

s: Rhesus be dispatched by some foul secret stroke
q: CHA. Our host is utterly destroyed, our king Hath been despatched by some foul secret stroke.

s: Rhesus’s funeral and apotheosis not plunge into the yawning grave
q: MUSE. They shall not plunge him in the yawning grave, Such vows will I address to Pluto’s bride, Daughter of fruitful Ceres, to release His ghost from the drear shades beneath

s: Ulysses is son of Laertes
q: Son of Laertes, O conceal your sword

s: Hector is a Trojan leader
q: HEC. O ye accursed authors of this mischief, How did those spies, who by the foe were sent Thus, to your infamy, escape, and spread Dire havoc through the host;

s: Hector is brother of Paris
q: PAR. General and brother, Hector, thee I call:

s: Hector places Rhesus (outside the Phrygian lines until morning)
q: MIN. Near at hand, And separate from the Phrygian troops, he lies; Hector hath placed him just without the lines Till morn arise;

s: Paris be a Phrygian
q: DIO. Then to Æneas will we go, or Paris That Phrygian most abhorred, and with our swords Lop off their heads.

s: Paris is brother of Hector
q: PAR. General and brother, Hector, thee I call:

s: Paris is protected by Venus (in battle)
q: MIN. Be of good cheer; for Venus Protects you: I in all your battles feel An interest, mindful of the prize I gained Favoured by you, and am for ever grateful:

s: the Muse is mother of Rhesus (his grieving mother)
q: for I a Muse Who by the wise am worshipped, hither come, One of the nine famed sisters, having seen The wretched fate of this my dearest son

s: the Muse is sister of the Muses (one of the nine sisters)
q: One of the nine famed sisters

s: the Greeks return to the fleet
q: ULY. To the fleet Let us in haste return:

s: Ulysses is ally of Diomede (in the night raid)
q: ULY. Either do thou, O Diomede, transpierce The Thracian soldiers, or to me consign That task; meanwhile seize thou the steeds.

s: the Thracians are allies of Trojans (in the Trojan War)
q: CHA. O dire calamity Of Troy’s allies, the Thracians!

s: Chorus of Trojan sentinels be stationed at here (to watch the camp)
q: Who should be punished But you? for you, I say, were stationed here To watch the camp

s: Rhesus’s Thracian army is destroyed in Rhesus’s death (during the night attack)
q: CHA. Our host is utterly destroyed, our king Hath been despatched by some foul secret stroke.

s: the Trojan camp is threatened by Rhesus’s Thracian army (if Rhesus survives the night)
q: If he outlives this night, nor Ajax, Nor can Achilles hinder him from wasting The camp of Greece

s: the Trojan night raid ask Was this Ulysses’ enterprise, or whose?
q: 1st SEMICHOR. Was this Ulysses’ enterprise, or whose?

s: fate and the Destinies forbid Ulysses (from killing Hector)
q: MIN. You can no more, the Destinies forbid: For Hector must not perish by your hand;

s: Chorus is composed of Chorus of Trojan sentinels
q: CHOR. Come on, strike, strike, destroy. Who marches yonder? Look, look, ’tis him I mean! these are the robbers Who in the dead of night alarmed our host.

s: Ulysses is supported by Minerva (through many toils)
q: ULY. Dread goddess, O Minerva, I distinguished Thy well-known voice: for midst unnumbered toils Thou ever dost support me:

s: Ulysses possesses Dolon’s weapons and clothing (taken after Dolon’s death)
q: ULY. What means this language? hast thou not performed A great exploit? have we not slain the spy Who to our navy went, and are not these The spoils of Dolon?

s: Ulysses kills Rhesus (during the Trojan night raid)
q: Although the gods forbid you to destroy Hector or Paris, heard ye not that Rhesus, A mighty chief, with numerous troops is come To Troy? If he outlives this night, nor Ajax, Nor can Achilles hinder him from wasting The camp of Greece, demolishing your walls, And forcing a wide passage through your gates With his victorious spear: him slay, and all Is yours

s: Diomede be seized by vain alarm
q: DIO. No; but the steely trappings which are linked To yonder chariots, rattled, and I too With vain alarm was seized,

s: Minerva is a goddess
q: ULY. Dread goddess, O Minerva, I distinguished Thy well-known voice:

s: Neptune come to hither
q: I Neptune hither come.

s: Hecuba is a queen (former queen of Troy)
q: Arise, thou wretch, and from the dust uplift Thy drooping head; though Ilion be no more, And thou a queen no longer

s: Hecuba is a captive (enslaved after Troy’s fall)
q: Here, alas! I sit In my loathed prison, Agamemnon’s tent; From princely mansions dragged, an aged slave

s: Hecuba is mother of Cassandra
q: My daughter, cast the sacred keys away

s: Hecuba is allotted to Ulysses (by the captives’ lottery)
q: By lot the king Of Ithaca Ulysses hath obtained you.

s: Cassandra is a prophetess (inspired by Apollo)
q: That spotless virgin too whom from his shrine Apollo with prophetic gifts inspired, Cassandra

s: Cassandra be bride of Agamemnon
q: Thou bride of Agamemnon

s: Cassandra is a captive (taken by Agamemnon)
q: Her the royal Agamemnon His chosen prize hath taken.

s: Cassandra is concubine of Agamemnon (against her former celibate priesthood)
q: No slave, But concubine.

s: Neptune builds Troy (with Apollo)
q: For round the fields Of Ilion, since Apollo and myself With symmetry exact reared many a tower Hewn from the solid rock

s: Cassandra is engaged to Agamemnon (in her prophetic vision of their marriage)
q: that king Of Greece, famed Agamemnon, shall in me Take to his arms a bride more inauspicious Than even Helen’s self

s: Cassandra retain my chastity unsullied
q: I leave those feasts the scenes of past delight, Torn from my brows avaunt, for I retain My chastity unsullied still; the winds To thee shall waft them, O prophetic king.

s: Cassandra prophesies Agamemnon’s death (after becoming his bride)
q: him will I smite, And lay his palace waste, in great revenge For my slain sire and brothers.

s: Cassandra prophesies Ulysses (that he will endure a ten-year return and later calamities)
q: Ten more long years elapsed beyond the term Spent in besieging Ilion, he alone Shall reach his country

s: Andromache is a captive (assigned after Troy’s fall)
q: How fares it with the lost Andromache? TAL. Her to Achilles’ son hath from the band Of captives chosen.

s: Talthybius is a herald (of the Grecian host)
q: O Hecuba, full oft, you know, to Troy I, as their herald, by the Grecian host Have been despatched

s: Talthybius announces lottery assigning the captives (to Hecuba and the Trojan women)
q: The lots are cast Already

s: Talthybius delivers Cassandra’s relationship with Agamemnon (as the Grecian herald)
q: Her the royal Agamemnon His chosen prize hath taken.

s: Helen is a captive (held among the Trojan captives)
q: Justly deemed A captive, among them is Spartan Helen

s: Agamemnon is a leader (of the Grecian host)
q: For the dread chieftain of the Grecian host, The son of Atreus

s: Neptune loves Troy (despite its destruction)
q: the love I bore The city where my Phrygian votaries dwelt, Laid waste by Greece, where smoke e’en now ascends The heavens, hath ne’er been rooted from this breast

s: Agamemnon loves Cassandra (with boundless passion despite her madness)
q: For the dread chieftain of the Grecian host, The son of Atreus, loves with boundless passion This damsel frantic as the Mænades.

s: Ulysses obtains Hecuba (by the captives’ lottery)
q: By lot the king Of Ithaca Ulysses hath obtained you.

s: Ilion be prosperous prosperous (once)
q: farewell, Thou city prosperous once

s: Troy be prosperous prosperous (once)
q: farewell, Thou city prosperous once; ye splendid towers

s: Troy sack This city (after ten years)
q: the leaders of the host that sacked This city, wait but for a prosperous breeze, That after ten years absence they their wives And children may with joy behold.

s: the Greeks is a army (that sacked Troy)
q: the leaders of the host that sacked This city

s: Greek homeward voyage make inauspicious Their journey home
q: Their journey home I am resolved to make Most inauspicious.

s: Neptune abandons Troy (because its temples are deserted)
q: I leave Troy the renowned, and my demolished shrines. For when pernicious solitude extends O’er cities her inexorable sway, Abandoned are the temples of the gods, None comes to worship there.

s: storm and dispersal of the Greek fleet is caused by Neptune (with violent waves and whirlpools)
q: My storms shall rouse Th’ Ægean deep; the shores of Myconè, Scyros with Lemnos, all the Delian rocks, And steep Caphareus with full many a corse Will I o’erspread.

s: the Trojan Horse is constructed by Epeus (under Minerva’s inspiration)
q: Epeus, by Minerva’s arts inspired, Framed with a skilful hand, and through the gates Sent that accursed machine, the horse which teemed With ambushed javelins.

s: Neptune allies with Minerva (to punish the Greeks)
q: but join your aid, Cause the Ægean deep with threefold waves, And ocean’s whirlpools horribly to rage

s: Minerva be leagued with Juno (in Phrygia’s overthrow)
q: Subdued By Juno, Argive goddess, and Minerva, Who leagued in Phrygia’s overthrow

s: Minerva inspires Epeus (to construct the Trojan Horse)
q: For on Parnassus bred, the Phocian chief Epeus, by Minerva’s arts inspired, Framed with a skilful hand, and through the gates Sent that accursed machine, the horse which teemed With ambushed javelins.

s: Minerva is insulted by Ajax (through the violation of her temple)
q: Know you not the insult Which hath been shown to me, and to my temple? NEP. I know that Ajax violently tore Cassandra thence.

s: Minerva smite The Greeks (with Jove’s thunderbolts)
q: For Jove will send down rain, immoderate hail, And pitchy blasts of air: he promises To give me too his thunderbolts to smite The Greeks and fire their ships

s: Hecuba be married to a mighty king (born to regal state)
q: Born to regal state, And with a mighty king in wedlock joined

s: Andromache is a captive (carried to Greece)
q: Hence with my son, A captive am I hurried; noble birth Subject to these vicissitudes now sinks Into degrading slavery

s: Andromache is forced to marry Neoptolemus (after Hector’s death)
q: for when I became A captive, Neoptolemus resolved To take me to his bed

s: Andromache is the widow of Hector (after his death)
q: But thou art slain, and I to Greece must sail A captive

s: Astyanax is a son Hector
q: Close follows her beloved Astyanax, The son of Hector

s: Astyanax is a grandson (of Hecuba)
q: O child, thou son Of my unhappy Hector, from thy mother And me thou unexpectedly art torn

s: Astyanax is sentenced to death death
q: They resolve To slay thy son

s: Astyanax’s execution is a execution (by being thrown from Troy’s towers)
q: He from the towers of Ilion must be thrown

s: Hector is a warrior (the bravest of the Phrygians)
q: O thou who erst wert Hector’s wife, that bravest Of Phrygians

s: Hector has house Hector’s house
q: In Hector’s house I acted as behoves each virtuous dame

s: Hector is the father of Astyanax (his surviving son)
q: Saying they ought not to train up the son Of that heroic sire

s: Hecuba is a mother (of Hector and the Trojan royal children)
q: Me, who am Hector’s mother

s: Hector’s death is a death of Hector (slaughtered)
q: O my daughter, cease to name the fate Of slaughtered Hector, whom no tears can save

s: Polyxena is a daughter (of Hecuba)
q: Polyxena, thy daughter, at the tomb Of Peleus’ son hath breathed her last

s: Polyxena is sacrificed at Achilles’ tomb (as a gift to the dead)
q: Polyxena, thy daughter, at the tomb Of Peleus’ son hath breathed her last, a gift To the deceased

s: Polyxena’s sacrifice is slain at bloody altars
q: To bloody altars dragged by impious hands, Alas! alas! how basely wert thou slain

s: Talthybius is a messenger (of the Greeks)
q: O thou who erst wert Hector’s wife, that bravest Of Phrygians, hate me not; for with reluctance Will I the general sentence of the Greeks And Pelops’ progeny, announce

s: Talthybius announces Astyanax’s execution (to Andromache and Hecuba)
q: They resolve To slay thy son; thou hear’st my dismal errand

s: Neoptolemus is a son (of Achilles)
q: With which Achilles’ son from Ilion’s siege Triumphant, will the Phthian temples grace

s: Neoptolemus takes as wife Andromache (after the fall of Troy)
q: Neoptolemus resolved To take me to his bed

s: Ulysses causes Astyanax’s execution (by persuading the assembled Greeks)
q: By his harangues to the assembled Greeks, Ulysses hath prevailed

s: Hecuba is a slave (after the fall of Troy)
q: But last of all, to crown My woes, an aged slave, shall I be borne To Greece

s: Ilion is no more Ilion
q: Now are those prosperous days No more; and Ilion is no more

s: Ilion is destroyed Those battlements (with devouring flame)
q: Those battlements which Phœbus’ self did rear The victor wasted with devouring flame

s: the fall and destruction of Troy is caused by the wooden horse deception (through Greek treachery)
q: The vehicle of many a daring Greek, Who burst like thunder from that wooden steed

s: the Trojan Horse is a wooden vehicle (concealing armed Greek soldiers)
q: The vehicle of many a daring Greek, Who burst like thunder from that wooden steed, With gorgeous trappings graced, in mimic state, Concealing armed bands

s: hope persists life (while life remains)
q: For the deceased are nothing: but fair hope, While life remains, can never be extinct

s: fate and the Destinies controls human fortunes (without human control)
q: Uncontrolled The power of fate

s: grief and mourning is a relief (for those who suffer)
q: To those who suffer, what a sweet relief Do tears afford! the sympathetic Muse Inspires their plaints

s: Hecuba loses Priam (her husband, slain at the altar of Hercæan Jove)
q: The venerable Priam, I bewailed not, From being told of his calamitous fate By others, but these eyes beheld him slain, E’en at the altar of Hercæan Jove

s: slavery is a condition degrading slavery (for noble birth)
q: noble birth Subject to these vicissitudes now sinks Into degrading slavery

s: Hecuba loses Polyxena (her daughter, sacrificed at Achilles’ tomb)
q: Polyxena, thy daughter, at the tomb Of Peleus’ son hath breathed her last, a gift To the deceased

s: Hecuba is attended by Hecuba’s attendants (after the fall of Troy)
q: Attendants of the aged Hecuba, Behold ye not your mistress

s: Andromache is a mother (of Astyanax)
q: Eager to cling to the maternal breast Close follows her beloved Astyanax, The son of Hector

s: Menelaus is a Greek
q: For I am he who long Endured the toils of battle, Menelaus, Attended by the Grecian host.

s: Helen is wedded to Deiphobus (against her will, according to her defense)
q: But a new husband, fierce Deiphobus, Obtained me for a wife by brutal force

s: Helen defends herself against Hecuba’s accusation of Helen (by attributing responsibility to the gods and others)
q: to each malignant charge With which, O Hecuba, I know thou com’st Prepared against me, will I make reply

s: Helen attributes her departure to Venus (claiming divine compulsion)
q: impute the guilt To Venus, and assume a power, beyond E’en that of Jove, who rules th’ inferior gods But yields to her behests.

s: Helen is accused of adultery (by Hecuba and Menelaus)
q: As that illustrious stem Whence thou deriv’st thy birth, and as thy rank Demand, on thy adulterous wife inflict Just punishment

s: Hecuba is a queen (of Troy)
q: O my Queen, Assert thy children’s and thy country’s cause

s: Hecuba is the mother of Paris
q: That evil genius, sprung from Hecuba, Distinguish him by either name you list, Paris or Alexander

s: Hecuba advocates execution of every woman who betrays Her lord
q: By slaying her, prepare for Greece the wreaths It merits, and extend to the whole sex This law, that every woman who betrays Her lord shall die.

s: Paris is the son of Hecuba
q: That evil genius, sprung from Hecuba, Distinguish him by either name you list, Paris or Alexander

s: Paris is the son of Priam
q: Did aged Priam ruin Troy and me, When erst that infant he forbore to slay

s: Paris is a judge (in the Judgment of Paris)
q: by Paris were the claims Of the three rival goddesses decided.

s: Menelaus is considered the husband of Helen (formerly and controversially)
q: But I am come to bear That Spartan dame away, whom with regret I term my consort, though she once was mine.

s: Venus promises as reward me
q: But Venus, who in rapturous terms extolled My charms, engaged that as the great reward She would on him bestow me

s: Venus promises Helen (as a reward to Paris for judging her the fairest)
q: She would on him bestow me; to her beauty If o’er each goddess he the preference gave.

s: Venus is considered more powerful than Jove (by Helen’s defense)
q: assume a power, beyond E’en that of Jove, who rules th’ inferior gods But yields to her behests.

s: Jove is identified as dread necessity (or that soul which animates The breasts of mortals)
q: whosoe’er thou art, Impervious to our reason, whether thou, O Jove, art dread necessity which rules All nature, or that soul which animates The breasts of mortals

s: Jove rules the inferior gods (according to Helen’s defense)
q: Jove, who rules th’ inferior gods But yields to her behests.

s: Chorus is a group of Phrygian women (mourning Troy’s destruction)
q: But ha! on this devoted realm are hurled Successive woes. Ye hapless Phrygian dames

s: Chorus supports Hecuba (in opposing Helen)
q: Assert thy children’s and thy country’s cause, ’Gainst her persuasive language

s: Menelaus is related to the Grecian host (as its leader or principal participant in the war)
q: For I am he who long Endured the toils of battle, Menelaus, Attended by the Grecian host.

s: the Greeks redeem Helen (by their arms after the fall of Troy)
q: for the troops Whose arms redeemed her, have to me consigned

s: Phrygians are defeated by the Greeks (in the war against Troy)
q: He and his country by the spear of Greece Have been destroyed.

s: Troy is destroyed by fire
q: For Troy, by fire consumed, lies level with the plain.

s: the Trojan War benefits Greece
q: for the benefits through me derived To Greece, I in the stead of laureate wreaths With slavery am requited.

s: the judgment of Paris awards victory to Venus (over Juno and Minerva)
q: Venus, o’er Minerva And Juno, gained the triumph

s: hospitality requires Helen’s execution (as demanded by Hecuba and the Chorus)
q: By slaying her, prepare for Greece the wreaths It merits, and extend to the whole sex This law, that every woman who betrays Her lord shall die.

s: Helen’s execution is to be slain she (in Argos’ lands)
q: But soon as she in Argos’ lands, with shame, As she deserves, shall she be slain

s: Greek homeward voyage is intended for Helen (as a captive transported from Troy)
q: o’er the foaming waves to Greece Will I convey her

s: Astyanax is killed by the Greeks (thrown from Troy’s towers)
q: Behold the slain Astyanax, whom Greece With rage inhuman from yon towers hath thrown.

s: Menelaus comes to punish Paris (for violating hospitality and taking Helen)
q: To Troy, Not in a woman’s cause, as many deem, I came, but came to punish him who broke The laws of hospitality, and ravished My consort from my palace

s: Astyanax’s execution is killed by Greece (from yon towers)
q: Behold the slain Astyanax, whom Greece With rage inhuman from yon towers hath thrown.

s: Menelaus has authority over Helen (the Greek army entrusted her disposition to him)
q: for the troops Whose arms redeemed her, have to me consigned That I might either take away, or spare Her life, and waft her to the Argive coast.

s: Menelaus plans to convey Helen (from Troy to Greece)
q: I am resolved that Helen shall not bleed In Troy, but o’er the foaming waves to Greece Will I convey her

s: Helen is a Spartan woman
q: But I am come to bear That Spartan dame away

s: Helen is a captive Phrygians (held among the defeated Trojan women)
q: But she beneath these tents is with the rest Of Phrygia’s captives numbered

s: Helen is considered the wife of Menelaus (former consort)
q: whom with regret I term my consort, though she once was mine.

s: Polydore is a son (of Hecuba and Priam)
q: come I Polydore, the son Of Hecuba from royal Cisseus sprung, And Priam

s: Hecuba is a queen (formerly queen of Troy)
q: Support your fellow-servant, once your queen

s: Hecuba is a daughter (of Cisseus)
q: come I Polydore, the son Of Hecuba from royal Cisseus sprung

s: Hecuba is a mother of Polyxena
q: The vision I abhor, which I in sleep This night have seen, relating to my son, Who here is fostered in the Thracian realm, And to Polyxena my dearest daughter

s: Hecuba is enslaved by the Greeks (after the fall of Troy)
q: by their victorious arms the Greeks Have made me captive

s: Hecuba is a woman A weak old woman
q: A weak old woman

s: Hecuba has dream The vision (in sleep)
q: The vision I abhor, which I in sleep This night have seen

s: Hecuba pleads for My daughter (not ... slay the maid)
q: O tear not My daughter from these arms, nor slay the maid

s: Polyxena is a daughter (of Hecuba)
q: O my daughter, if thy power exceed Thy mother’s

s: Polyxena is a sister of Hector
q: the sister Of Hector, and full many a valiant chief

s: Polydore is a youngest of Priam’s sons
q: I was the youngest of all Priam’s sons

s: Polyxena is a princess (of Troy)
q: ye shades receive A princess.

s: Polyxena is sacrificed at the tomb of Peleus’ son (by the Greeks)
q: The Greeks, with one consent, Resolve that on the tomb of Peleus’ son Thou shalt be sacrificed.

s: Polyxena is subject to Polyxena’s sacrifice (at Achilles’ tomb)
q: The Greeks, with one consent, Resolve that on the tomb of Peleus’ son Thou shalt be sacrificed.

s: Polyxena chooses death (rather than servitude and dishonor)
q: I’ll not call down the wrath Of Jove who guards the suppliant, but will follow Thy steps, because necessity ordains And ’tis my wish to die

s: Ulysses is a son of Laertes (Greek commander and orator)
q: he, that crafty orator, endued With sweetest voice, the favourite of the crowd, Laertes’ son

s: Ulysses is a Greek (member of the Greek army)
q: Th’ unwelcome tidings; at Achilles’ tomb, Polyxena, thy daughter, have the Greeks Resolved to slay; me to attend the virgin Have they commanded

s: Ulysses is ordered to escort Polyxena (to her sacrifice)
q: me to attend the virgin Have they commanded

s: Ulysses persuades the Greeks (to honor Achilles by accepting the sacrifice)
q: Laertes’ son, persuaded all the host, Not to reject the first of Grecian chiefs

s: Achilles is a greek chief the first of Grecian chiefs
q: the first of Grecian chiefs

s: Achilles is dead death (having died for Greece)
q: Achilles claims such homage, who for Greece Died nobly.

s: Polydore is sent to Polymestor (secretly, as a child and royal refugee)
q: from Phrygia’s realm In privacy conveyed me to the house Of Polymestor, of his Thracian friend

s: Achilles has tomb Achilles’ tomb
q: at Achilles’ tomb
